trans-unit.source: Control-plane tokens grant browserless access to the admin port with your powers. They are the foundation for a Meerkat CLI and MCP server, which let an AI or a script manage the gateway. That tooling is planned; the tokens work today for your own automation.
Shown once: copy it now, it cannot be retrieved later.
An identity provider the browser is sent to. The token it returns is verified against its published keys, so nothing is taken on trust.
A directory asked directly, with what the person typed in the ordinary sign-in form. No button appears on the login page.

GitHub proves the account, but signs nothing: there is no token to verify, so the trust rests on the exchange and on TLS. Restrict the organisations below unless you mean to open the door to every GitHub account.
Register an OAuth app on GitHub with these two addresses, then paste back the Client ID and the secret it gives you.
Create an OAuth app on GitHub
These addresses come from the one you reached this gateway by. In production, register the public domain name instead: a vendor handed a localhost sends everyone back to a machine that is not yours.
What the login page shows on the button
The segment of the sign-in URL, derived from the authority
Its discovery document is read from there
Comma separated, empty accepts every address the authority knows
Comma separated. Empty lets in ANY GitHub account.
These organisations and teams also come back as groups — "org" for an organisation, "org/team" for a team — which a tenant's group rule can turn into roles.
ldaps is the one to use unless the directory is on a private network
Used to SEARCH, never to sign anyone in
%s is what the person typed; empty uses the dialect's default
Create an account on first sign-in
The account is created empty and reaches nothing: an administrator then places it in an organization and grants roles. Off, only people already linked may come in.
The accounts that sign in through it will keep existing, but will no longer have a way in.

Every door into the data plane, the accounts held here included. An authority proves who someone is; it never decides what they may do: a first sign-in creates an account that reaches nothing until an administrator places it in an organization and grants roles. Switch them all off and nobody signs in to the data plane, which is what a gateway serving public routes only may want.
The passwords held here. Off, only the other authorities answer; this console always keeps its own password sign-in.

Routes, roles, authorities, mail relay, themes and gateway settings travel as one file. Users, organisations, sessions and the vault stay where they are: they are not configuration, they are what this gateway lives with.

A secret leaves as its vault reference or not at all, so the file is safe to put in a ticket or a git repository. Two exports of the same configuration are the same bytes, which is what makes the difference between two of them worth reading.
users, organisations and their members, sessions, the vault, the audit trail, personal tokens, signing keys
These secrets are stored here as values rather than vault references, so they will NOT be in the file. Wherever it lands, the fields will be empty.

The file references these vault entries. On the other side, one that already exists is used as it stands; one that is missing is created EMPTY and reported, and whatever references it stays inert until someone fills it. Nothing is overwritten and nothing blocks the import.
A zip: the configuration reads and diffs, the logo sits beside it as a file.
Nothing is applied before you have seen what would change. What the file does not mention is left alone, and a secret it does not carry keeps the one already stored.
Remove what the file does not mention
Only inside the sections the file actually carries: a file holding routes alone never touches the roles.
This file describes what is already configured here. Importing it would change nothing.
This configuration expects vault entries that do not exist here. They will be created empty, and a route that references an empty entry does not serve until it is filled.

A coherent copy of the whole database, taken while the gateway runs: routes and vault, but also users, organisations, sessions and the audit trail. This is what a backup restores; a configuration export is what a second gateway reproduces.

Meerkat takes the snapshot, because copying a live database with cp can catch it mid-write and nothing says so until the day you restore it. Scheduling, retention and shipping it off the host belong to your backup tool, not here.

Restoring happens with the service stopped: a database cannot be replaced under the process holding it open, and the sessions and users it brings back are the ones the request doing it would depend on. Keep the old file until the new one has proven itself.
The master key of this gateway comes from MEERKAT_VAULT_KEY, so it is not in that directory: the snapshot holds the vault encrypted and is worth nothing without that variable. Keep it that way.

The master key sits next to the database. Backing them up together undoes the encryption at rest, exactly as a vault file stored beside its passphrase would: keep the key in a secret manager, or supply it through MEERKAT_VAULT_KEY.
The import created these empty. This is the moment to fill them: in a week nobody remembers what they were for.
The SMTP server that delivers account e-mails: confirmations, password resets, administrator notifications. The sender address lives here because a provider only accepts the account it authenticated.
. The name in front of the address is set in the application settings.
A token minted by client credentials stands in for the password (XOAUTH2). This is the only way into Microsoft 365, which no longer accepts a password over SMTP.
An account and a secret. What every transactional relay uses, and what Gmail still accepts with an application password.
Empty sends as the account. Most providers accept only that address, or a verified alias.
The account is not an address, so one is required here. It must be verified with the provider.

Every entry you administer, encrypted under this passphrase. Unlike a configuration export, this file holds the values themselves: do not version it, and delete it once it has been used. Store the passphrase in a password manager: without it nobody reads the file, not even Meerkat.
An entry that is missing here is created, one that was left empty is filled, and one that already holds a different value is left alone unless you say otherwise.
Replace entries that already hold a different value
left alone: they already hold a different value
skipped: not yours to write, or an unknown organisation
Every value the configuration refers to, in one place. Use one anywhere with $name: secrets are encrypted and never shown again, plain values stay readable.
No entry yet. Add the first one.
No authority is linked and this account has no local password: it cannot sign in. Link it to an authority, or set a password.
This account signs in with its local password only.
No roles in the catalogue yet: create them in Application / Roles.
Owns the tenant: transfer it in the Danger zone
Administers this tenant: groups, members, hours
A role still granted by a group cannot be deleted: remove it from the groups first.
The catalogue itself: what hangs here is a top-level role.
No role yet: the + on the row above creates the first one.
Cumulative merges the roles of every assigned group; exclusive makes members pick ONE group when they enter this tenant.
Exactly as the authority spells it. Leave empty for anyone from that authority.
No group reported yet: nobody has signed in through an authority that sends any.
Name an authority, an upstream group, or both. A rule matching everything would admit anyone the gateway ever authenticates, through an authority added later for something else.
A tenant has a single owner. The chosen member becomes it. Ownership is independent of membership, so the previous owner keeps their membership unchanged.
Removes the tenant, its memberships and its groups. There is no undo.
Type the tenant name to confirm

What an authority says about someone, turned into access here. A rule reads: whoever arrives with this group upstream becomes a member of this organization, with this group. Nothing else is taken from the authority, and a rule can only grant what belongs here.
For a directory carrying a group per site:
group here. For an organization with its OWN directory, leave the upstream group empty: anyone who signs in through that authority becomes a member.
No authority is enabled yet. These rules act on what an authority reports, so there is nothing to map until one is configured (Infra, Authentication).
This organization has no group yet. Create one first: a rule grants a group, and the roles it carries are what someone may actually do here.
No rule yet: everyone arriving through an authority waits for an administrator to place them.
What it granted is taken back the next time each person signs in. Anyone an administrator placed by hand stays.
Administers the whole gateway: routes, users, tenants, settings
Administers the routing plane: routes and the built-in pages
Administers the application identity: users, roles, settings
Unlocks the developer tooling: dev keys, service substitution (plug)
Can opt into a developer's variant of the application
May create tenants, and owns the tenants they create
They will be signed out and will not be able to sign in again until you enable them.
Users get a "Report an issue" entry in their user button, where that button is on the page.
The report, its screenshot and its comments will be permanently removed.
Match the request path; several patterns act as a logical OR
A header is present, optionally matching a regexp
A cookie is present, optionally matching a regexp
A query parameter is present, optionally matching a regexp
The client address is in CIDR ranges
The last X-Forwarded-For address is in CIDR ranges
Split traffic between the routes of a group (canary)
Remove the first N path segments
Prepend a prefix to the path
Rewrite the path with a regexp
Set a request header, replacing the client value
Set a response header, replacing the upstream value
Answer with a redirect instead of proxying
Answer 503 with a gateway maintenance page
Copy a request header into another name
Rewrite a query parameter with a regexp
Force the Host header sent to the service
Send the client Host header instead of the upstream one
Refuse requests bigger than a limit
Stop calling a failing service, with a fallback
Retry idempotent requests on upstream errors
Rewrite a response header with a regexp
Fix the Location header of upstream redirects
Answer a fixed status and body
No gateway rule — delegated to the API backend
Meerkat adds no gate: the upstream keeps its own security. Not the same as public.
Open to everyone, signed in or not.
Anyone with an account, including one that belongs to no organisation yet.
An organisation must be active on the session. Turns away an account still awaiting access.
The active organisation must be one of those named below.
Held in the active organisation. Left empty, any role passes.
An exception, not a level: they pass whatever is required above.

Gate an API's operations at the gateway, straight from its OpenAPI spec: prototype roles before wiring them into the backend, centralize access control, or protect a backend you cannot modify. An operation you leave untouched keeps being secured by the backend itself.
No route exposes an OpenAPI spec yet. Add a Swagger URL to an API route, then come back here.
Rules set here are enforced by the gateway. Where nothing is set, security stays delegated to the API backend.
Applied in order to the request before it reaches the service.
Applied in order to the response before it reaches the client.
Answers instead of proxying (redirect, maintenance): at most one, not combined with other modifiers.
None: the route proxies to its upstream.
What the upstream receives on every request of this route, for a sample caller. Values are fictional; the shape, the names and the signature are the real ones.
Trust the first X-Forwarded-For entry (only behind a trusted proxy)
No predicates yet: the route matches nothing.
Ignored: a redirect answers this route
The OpenAPI spec the service exposes, for endpoint-level security and swagger UI
When set, this app shows in the user's apps menu (if their access allows it), under this name.
The route's base access, applied to the whole route. Leave it empty to delegate security to the upstream; set it to gate at the edge. An API route can refine it per operation in Endpoint security.
Forwards the signed-in caller to the service behind this route. Pick a transport, then choose which facts travel and, optionally, the name each one takes on the way out.
The gateway signs each token; backends verify it against the published JWKS. Manage the keys with "Signing keys" on the Routes page.
What to include in the payload (everything by default):
Injects the meerkat-user-button web component into the pages: profile, tenant switch, languages, color scheme, sign out.
Does the application support a color scheme? The choice is always reflected on the CSS color-scheme and a data-meerkat-scheme attribute; pick the application's own mechanism on top if it has one.
Offer the color-scheme switch (reflected on the page for the application)
The application's locale offer, managed in Application General. Uncheck the ones this UI does not support: they leave the button's menu and the forwarding.
Accept-Language is ALWAYS sent, rewritten with the user's choice in first position. Extra mechanisms ride on top, cumulative.
Puts the user's effective roles on the page: classes or a custom attribute on a tag of your choice, or a meta tag, so the application can gate elements on roles with pure CSS.
Exposes the selected user facts to the PAGE, as attributes on a tag of your choice or as meta tags. To send the user to the service itself, use the Identity section: both apply at once.
A style block injected into the pages: tweak the application's look from the gateway.
A script injected into the pages, right after the head opens.
Sent as a comma-separated string (click for a JSON array)
Sent as a JSON array (click for a comma-separated string)
A header, cookie or query matcher needs a name
Weight needs both a group and a weight
Describe a request: the gateway replays it through the live routing table and names the route that takes it. Nothing is sent to any upstream.
disabled: not in the live routing table
not evaluated: a route above already matched
No route matches: the gateway would answer 404.
No route yet, create the first one.

The gateway signs each identity token with its private key (which never leaves the server). Backends fetch this JWKS once, cache it, and verify each token by its key id. Rotation is then picked up on its own.
Static fallback: paste the PEM of your route's algorithm into that backend.
Rotate now? Old keys stay valid briefly (grace window).
Every administrative change, with the exact fields that moved and their before and after.
No audit events for this filter.
The application-wide access window: every tenant inherits it unless it defines its own.

The locales your APPLICATION supports (ISO codes like fr or fr-FR). They fill the flow pages and the user button, and the signed-in user's choice follows every proxied request. Empty leaves the flow pages in English.
No application locale yet. The flow pages speak English.
"" is not a valid ISO code
Require a second factor for every user. Organizations and members can override this.
How long a session lives before the user must sign in again.
The name shown in front of the sender address. The address itself belongs to the mail relay, because a provider only lets you send as the account it authenticated.
Mail relay: not configured. Account e-mails cannot go out until an infra admin sets it up.
Throttles brute-force attempts: failed sign-ins per address and account within the window, and wrong two-factor codes per account. Zero disables a limiter.

Let visitors create their own account on the sign-in page. The address is confirmed by email, administrators are notified, and the account waits until someone grants it access. Requires a sender address above and a mail relay (Infra, Mail relay).
Let users register passkeys and sign in with them instead of the password and second factor.
Let users mint personal access tokens (Profile, Security) to call the API routes behind the gateway without a browser session. A token acts with the user's context at creation.
Let users skip the two-factor challenge on a browser they mark as trusted, until it expires.
A secret is not saved in clear. Move it into the vault to continue.
A secret is stored in clear in the configuration.
A secret is stored. Leave empty to keep it.
The secret stays where it is until you confirm, then only its name remains in the configuration. Give it a name you will recognise elsewhere.
Encrypted at rest and never shown again. Referenced by $name wherever it is needed.
Stored in clear and readable. Referenced by $name wherever it is needed.
A letter, then letters, digits, dot, dash or underscore
Leave empty to keep the stored secret
Drop your logo here, or click
Use a png, jpeg, webp or svg image
Decorative flow-page effects: the ambient halo behind the page, logo & button glows, and the app-name gradient. Uncheck for a flat design; this colour then goes unused.
